summary: A macro-enabled Excel attachment with an auto-execute macro arrived from a known vendor domain. The known sender is a benign signal, but an auto-executing macro in an unexpected financial statement is a common malware delivery method, and a compromised vendor account is possible. The alert has no sandbox result or authentication data, so the verdict cannot be confirmed either way.

evidence.why: The sender domain is a known vendor, which points toward legitimate business email.
A statement from an accounts mailbox is a plausible business email, but a compromised vendor account would look identical.
A macro-enabled .xlsm for a statement is unusual, because vendors typically send PDFs or plain .xlsx files. This points toward malicious activity.
Macros are a common way to deliver malware, which raises risk regardless of the sender.
The macro runs automatically on open, which is a strong malicious indicator and rarely justified in legitimate statements.

recommended_action.detail: Escalate to L2. Hold or quarantine the email if it has not been opened. Detonate the attachment in a sandbox and inspect the macro code. Contact the vendor through a known channel to confirm they sent it. Check whether any recipient has opened the file, and isolate any host that did.
